fc-1.definition: The throughput limitation caused by the shared single physical bus connecting the CPU to memory, which forces instructions and data to be transferred sequentially.
fc-1.example: Modern architectures mitigate this using multi-level cache hierarchies (L1, L2, L3) and separate instruction/data caches.

fc-2.definition: A dedicated software routine executed by the operating system when a hardware or software interrupt occurs, handling the trigger before resuming previous execution.
fc-2.example: When a key is pressed, the keyboard controller triggers an interrupt line and the OS dispatches the keyboard ISR.

fc-3.definition: A specialized electronic circuit composed of thousands of parallel execution cores optimized for performing simultaneous repetitive floating-point matrix calculations.
fc-3.example: Used for accelerating matrix multiplications in deep learning and 3D graphic rendering pipelines.

fc-4.definition: A transmission paradigm where data streams are split into independent packets routed dynamically across intermediary nodes based on optimal routing metrics.
fc-4.example: Contrasted with circuit switching where a dedicated physical communication path is occupied for the entire call.

fc-5.definition: A cryptographic protocol that provides end-to-end communications security over a computer network using asymmetric public key cryptography for handshakes and symmetric encryption for session payloads.
fc-5.example: Provides encryption, integrity checks, and authentication for HTTPS web traffic.

fc-6.definition: A database schema design standard where all relations are in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key.
fc-6.example: 'Every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key, so help me Codd.'

fc-7.definition: A relational constraint requiring that every foreign key value in a child table must match an existing primary key value in the referenced parent table or be NULL.
fc-7.example: Enforced with 'ON DELETE CASCADE' or 'ON DELETE RESTRICT' constraints in SQL.

fc-8.definition: An error scenario where an ML model learns the random noise and idiosyncrasies of its training set rather than the underlying pattern, degrading performance on unseen test data.
fc-8.example: Mitigated by regularization, dropout layers, early stopping, and data augmentation.

fc-9.definition: Systematic and repeatable errors in a computer system that generate unfair outcomes, often stemming from skewed or unrepresentative training data or flawed modeling assumptions.
fc-9.example: Facial recognition models performing with higher error rates on underrepresented demographic groups.

fc-10.definition: The breakdown of a complex problem, system, or algorithm into smaller, self-contained, and more manageable constituent components.
fc-10.example: Decomposing an e-commerce platform into catalog, shopping cart, authentication, and payment gateway modules.

fc-11.definition: An efficient search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted list by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half with O(log n) time complexity.
fc-11.example: Searching a sorted list of 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons.

fc-12.definition: A mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of an algorithm's execution time as the input size n grows towards infinity.
fc-12.example: Linear search is O(n), Bubble Sort is O(n²), and Merge Sort is O(n log n).

fc-13.definition: The bundling of data attributes and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class), while restricting direct access to internal components.
fc-13.example: Using private attributes (`__balance`) with public accessor methods (`deposit`, `withdraw`).

fc-14.definition: The ability of different object classes to respond to the same method call in distinct, class-specific ways through method overriding.
fc-14.example: A base class `Shape` defines `draw()`; subclasses `Circle` and `Square` implement custom `draw()` routines.

fc-15.definition: A linear data structure operating under the First-In-First-Out rule, where new elements are enqueued at the rear and elements are dequeued from the front.
fc-15.example: Printer spool queues and OS process ready queues.

fc-16.definition: A linear collection of elements with two principal operations: push (adds to top) and pop (removes from top), following the Last-In-First-Out discipline.
fc-16.example: Used in the call stack for managing function execution and recursion frames.

fc-cs-1.definition: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model: A generative deep learning framework that models data generation as the reverse of a progressive Gaussian noise injection Markov chain.
fc-cs-1.example: Visionary Studios art directors use DDPM to synthesize initial photorealistic campaign concepts from pure Gaussian noise.

fc-cs-2.definition: A class of generative models that learns to recover target data by estimating and subtracting injected noise across parameterized discrete timesteps.
fc-cs-2.example: Used for high-fidelity text-to-image synthesis by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise tensors over T=1000 timesteps.

fc-cs-3.definition: The deliberate, scheduled addition of Gaussian noise to an image tensor over timesteps t during the forward diffusion process.
fc-cs-3.example: At timestep T=1000 in the variance schedule βt, the original graphic x0 is transformed into isotropic Gaussian noise.

fc-cs-4.definition: The algorithmic estimation and removal of injected noise from a corrupted input representation, performed by a parameterized neural network (typically a U-Net).
fc-cs-4.example: The U-Net predicts the exact noise vector εθ added at timestep t, subtracting it from xt to recover xt-1.

fc-cs-5.definition: Image generation guided by explicit external constraints, such as natural language text prompts, class category labels, segmentation depth maps, or edge sketches.
fc-cs-5.example: Conditioning synthesis on 'luxury watch in minimalist marble studio' via cross-attention token embeddings.

fc-cs-6.definition: Generating novel samples purely from learned data distribution statistics without any external guiding prompts or class conditions.
fc-cs-6.example: Sampling randomly from isotropic Gaussian noise to generate diverse unguided landscape visuals.

fc-cs-7.definition: Synthesizing coherent spatial imagery conditioned on textual descriptions using multimodal semantic cross-attention embeddings (e.g. CLIP).
fc-cs-7.example: Translating natural language advertising copy into high-fidelity concept storyboard assets for Visionary Studios.

fc-cs-8.definition: Transforming an existing source visual representation into a target artistic style or domain while preserving underlying spatial geometry.
fc-cs-8.example: Converting rough client hand-sketched wireframes into photorealistic rendered product mockups.

fc-cs-9.definition: Mapping discrete words or visual patches into a continuous, dense, semantic vector space where distance corresponds to contextual conceptual similarity.
fc-cs-9.example: A CLIP text encoder converts prompt tokens into 768-dimensional normalized directional vectors.

fc-cs-10.definition: Systematically filtering, balancing, deduplicating, and auditing training data to ensure copyright compliance, artist permission, and representational fairness.
fc-cs-10.example: Visionary Studios audits image corpora to remove scraped uncredited artist portfolios and prevent IP infringement.

fc-cs-11.definition: Active algorithmic and statistical measures designed to identify and eliminate systematic skew, prejudice, or demographic stereotyping in AI generation.
fc-cs-11.example: Balancing training sets across demographic and cultural axes so generated professional roles avoid historical societal skew.

fc-cs-12.definition: Preserving identical facial identity, attire, proportions, and lighting of a subject across multiple distinct generated camera angles and scenes.
fc-cs-12.example: Using identity embeddings or LoRA adaptations to keep the same brand ambassador consistent across a multi-ad rollout.

fc-cs-13.definition: Convolutional Neural Network: A specialized deep architecture using spatial kernels with translation invariance, widely utilized in computer vision and GAN discriminators.
fc-cs-13.example: Feature extraction layers in the Inception-v3 classifier used to extract deep perceptual feature maps for FID calculations.

fc-cs-14.definition: Generative Adversarial Network: A two-player zero-sum minimax framework where a Generator and Discriminator compete against each other to produce synthetic outputs.
fc-cs-14.example: Using an adversarial discriminator patch loss to force super-resolution upscalers to produce photorealistic fine micro-textures.

fc-cs-15.definition: The two competing networks in a GAN: the Generator synthesizes fake samples from random noise, while the Discriminator acts as a binary classifier discerning real from fake.
fc-cs-15.example: Generator minimizes log(1 - D(G(z))) while Discriminator maximizes log D(x) + log(1 - D(G(z))).

fc-cs-16.definition: The continuous competitive optimization dynamic between Generator and Discriminator, converging toward a Nash equilibrium where the discriminator cannot distinguish authentic from synthetic data.
fc-cs-16.example: Both networks improve simultaneously until discriminator accuracy hovers at random guessing (D(x) = 0.5).

fc-cs-17.definition: A severe failure mode in GAN training where the Generator outputs only a narrow subset of realistic images that fools the Discriminator, ignoring the variety of the true dataset distribution.
fc-cs-17.example: Synthesizing only one specific car angle repeatedly across all vehicle prompts, destroying advertising campaign diversity.

fc-cs-18.definition: A compressed, lower-dimensional manifold representation where high-dimensional data (e.g. 1024x1024 images) is compactly encoded while retaining core perceptual semantics.
fc-cs-18.example: Compressing an image from 1024x1024x3 down to a 128x128x4 latent tensor to execute diffusion with 64x less computation.

fc-cs-19.definition: Variational Autoencoder: A probabilistic generative architecture that encodes input data into a parameterized latent Gaussian distribution and reconstructs it via a decoder.
fc-cs-19.example: The VAE encoder strips imperceptible high-frequency pixel noise before latent diffusion, while the decoder reconstructs crisp pixels.

fc-cs-20.definition: An architectural fusion combining distinct generative approaches (such as VAE perceptual compression + latent diffusion + GAN perceptual patch loss) to maximize fidelity while minimizing compute.
fc-cs-20.example: Latent Diffusion Models (LDM) marry VAE compression with U-Net score-based denoising to achieve fast, high-DPI generation.

fc-cs-21.definition: An exact-likelihood generative architecture utilizing invertible transformations with tractable Jacobian determinants to map directly between data and latent spaces.
fc-cs-21.example: Provides exact log-likelihood calculation and bijective mapping between pixel space and latent vectors without approximation.

fc-cs-22.definition: Fréchet Inception Distance: The gold standard metric evaluating synthetic imagery by calculating the Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussian feature distributions of real and fake images in deep feature space. Lower is better.
fc-cs-22.example: Visionary Studios measures FID against client reference photos; lower scores confirm high visual fidelity and diverse outputs.

fc-cs-23.definition: An early generative metric measuring conditional class confidence (sharpness) and marginal distribution entropy (diversity) on synthetic images alone, without reference to real images. Higher is better.
fc-cs-23.example: Unable to detect mode collapse when generated outputs are sharp, making it inferior to FID for commercial quality assurance.

q-a1-1.prompt: State one architectural difference between a central processing unit (CPU) and a graphics processing unit (GPU).
q-a1-1.hint: Consider the number of execution cores and the types of workloads they are optimized for (low-latency sequential vs high-throughput parallel).

markScheme.point: CPU: Engineered for low-latency sequential execution containing relatively few, high-performance cores with sophisticated control logic and large caches.
GPU: Engineered for high-throughput data-parallel execution containing hundreds or thousands of smaller, energy-efficient cores optimized for matrix and arithmetic operations.

q-a1-1.examinerTip: Avoid colloquial responses such as 'GPUs are for gaming'. Always emphasize architectural differences like sequential vs massively parallel execution cores.

q-a1-2.prompt: Explain the role of the Program Counter (PC), Memory Address Register (MAR), Memory Data Register (MDR), and Current Instruction Register (CIR) during the Fetch stage of the machine cycle.
q-a1-2.hint: Trace how the address moves from the PC across the address bus to fetch the instruction word into the processor.

markScheme.point: The Program Counter (PC) holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched; this address is copied to the Memory Address Register (MAR).
The Control Unit asserts a read signal on the control bus, loading the instruction data from RAM via the data bus into the Memory Data Register (MDR).
The PC is incremented to point to the subsequent sequential memory address.
The instruction is transferred from the MDR into the Current Instruction Register (CIR) where it will be decoded.

q-a1-2.examinerTip: Always explicitly mention that the PC is incremented during or immediately after the fetch step.

q-a1-3.prompt: Construct the truth table for the Boolean expression: X = (A AND B) NOR (NOT C).
q-a1-3.hint: Evaluate the terms step by step: first calculate (A AND B), then (NOT C), and finally invert the OR combination of both.

markScheme.point: Correct evaluation of sub-expression (A AND B) across all 8 combinations [1 mark].
Correct evaluation of (NOT C) across all 8 combinations [1 mark].
Final output column X is true (1) only when both (A AND B) is 0 and (NOT C) is 0 [i.e., C is 1 and not both A and B are 1] [1 mark].

q-a1-3.examinerTip: Ensure your truth table rows follow standard ascending binary order (000, 001, 010, ... 111) to avoid indexing mistakes.

q-a1-4.prompt: Compare the use of polling versus hardware interrupts for an embedded autonomous rover that monitors obstacle collision sensors.
q-a1-4.hint: Think about CPU cycles wasted during polling and latency requirements when an immediate collision avoidance maneuver is required.

markScheme.point: Polling repeatedly checks the sensor status in a loop, consuming valuable CPU cycles and power even when no obstacle is present.
Interrupts allow the processor to execute mission tasks uninterrupted until an obstacle trigger asserts a hardware line, providing deterministic, low-latency response.
For collision sensors, interrupts prevent buffer delay or missed triggers that could cause physical crashes.

q-a1-4.examinerTip: Highlight the real-time safety implications: polling latency could cause sensor overruns.

q-a1-5.prompt: Outline the four principal phases of compilation (lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation/optimization).
q-a1-5.hint: Trace how raw source code strings are tokenized, parsed into an abstract syntax tree (AST), type-checked, and finally converted to machine binaries.

markScheme.point: Lexical Analysis: Scans source characters, strips comments and whitespace, and groups lexemes into tokens while populating the symbol table.
Syntax Analysis: Validates token sequences against programming language grammar and constructs a Parse Tree or Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
Semantic Analysis: Checks type compatibility, variable declarations, and scope consistency across the symbol table.
Code Generation & Optimization: Emits intermediate/machine code and performs register allocation and dead-code elimination to improve speed.

q-a1-5.examinerTip: Clearly distinguish between syntax errors (violating grammar rules) and semantic errors (type mismatches or undeclared identifiers).

q-a2-1.prompt: Distinguish between a Local Area Network (LAN) and a Wide Area Network (WAN) in terms of geographical span and ownership of telecommunication infrastructure.
q-a2-1.hint: Consider who owns the transmission lines and whether the network is restricted to a single building/campus.

markScheme.point: Geographical Span: A LAN covers a small geographic area (e.g. single office, building, or school campus), whereas a WAN covers broad geographical areas (e.g. cities, nations, or continents).
Infrastructure Ownership: LAN hardware/cables are owned and administered directly by the organization; WAN connections rely on leased public telecommunications carriers/ISPs.

q-a2-1.examinerTip: Be precise regarding ownership: private vs leased/public telecommunication infrastructure.

q-a2-2.prompt: Describe how packet switching routes data across the Internet, mentioning packet headers, routing decisions, and destination reassembly.
q-a2-2.hint: Recall that data is split into independent units that can traverse different physical links.

markScheme.point: Data payload is divided into standardized chunks called packets, each prepended with a header containing source/destination IP addresses and sequence numbers.
Routers independently inspect headers and forward packets dynamically along optimal paths based on current network congestion and routing tables.
At the destination host, the TCP/IP stack checks checksums, re-orders packets using sequence numbers, and requests retransmission of dropped packets.

q-a2-2.examinerTip: Emphasize that packets can take completely different geographic routes and arrive out of order.

q-a2-3.prompt: Explain how asymmetric encryption and digital certificates guarantee both confidentiality and authentication during an HTTPS session establishment.
q-a2-3.hint: Contrast public key encryption for key exchange with certificate authority (CA) digital signatures.

markScheme.point: Digital Certificate: The server presents a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) containing its public key, verifying the authentic identity of the web domain.
Authentication: The client verifies the CA's digital signature using the CA's pre-installed public key, preventing man-in-the-middle spoofing.
Asymmetric Key Exchange: The client generates a random symmetric session key, encrypts it using the server's public key, and sends it to the server.
Confidentiality: Only the server holding the matching private key can decrypt this session key; subsequent traffic uses high-speed symmetric encryption.

q-a2-3.examinerTip: Make sure you explain why asymmetric encryption is used only for the initial handshake (performance overhead) while symmetric is used for streaming payload.

q-a3-1.prompt:
A student database contains a table with columns: (StudentID, StudentName, CourseCode, CourseTitle, InstructorName, InstructorOffice).

Explain why this table violates Second Normal Form (2NF) and Third Normal Form (3NF), and outline how to decompose it.
q-a3-1.hint: Identify the composite candidate key (StudentID, CourseCode), look for partial functional dependencies, and identify transitive dependencies.

markScheme.point: 2NF Violation: The primary key is composite (StudentID, CourseCode). StudentName depends only on StudentID, and CourseTitle depends only on CourseCode (partial functional dependency).
3NF Violation: InstructorOffice depends on InstructorName (non-key attribute determines another non-key attribute: transitive dependency).
Decomposition Step 1: Create separate Student table (StudentID, StudentName) and Course table (CourseCode, CourseTitle, InstructorID).
Decomposition Step 2: Create Instructor table (InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) and StudentEnrollment junction table (StudentID, CourseCode).

q-a3-1.examinerTip: Remember: 2NF requires removing partial dependencies on composite keys; 3NF requires removing transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.

q-a3-2.prompt:
Given two tables:
- Students (student_id, full_name, cohort_year)
- Scores (score_id, student_id, paper_number, marks_earned)

Write an SQL query to display the full_name and average marks earned for students in cohort_year '2026', showing only students whose average score exceeds 80, sorted descending by average mark.
q-a3-2.hint: Use an INNER JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING clause, and ORDER BY.
q-a3-2.codeSnippet:
SELECT Students.full_name, AVG(Scores.marks_earned) AS avg_mark
FROM Students
JOIN Scores ON Students.student_id = Scores.student_id
WHERE Students.cohort_year = '2026'
GROUP BY Students.student_id, Students.full_name
HAVING AVG(Scores.marks_earned) > 80
ORDER BY avg_mark DESC;

markScheme.point: Correct SELECT and INNER JOIN syntax connecting Students.student_id = Scores.student_id [1 mark].
Correct WHERE condition for cohort_year = '2026' and GROUP BY clause [1 mark].
Correct HAVING AVG(marks_earned) > 80 condition and ORDER BY DESC [1 mark].

q-a3-2.examinerTip: Remember that WHERE filters rows before aggregation, while HAVING filters aggregated group metrics.

q-a3-3.subtopicName: Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
q-a3-3.prompt: Evaluate when a document-oriented NoSQL database (such as MongoDB) is preferable over a strict relational database (RDBMS) for an IoT telemetry platform.
q-a3-3.hint: Consider schema flexibility, horizontal write-scaling, and polymorphic sensor payloads.

markScheme.point: Schema Flexibility: Different IoT sensor models emit varying telemetry schemas without requiring costly database ALTER TABLE migrations.
Horizontal Scalability: Document stores naturally shard across distributed server clusters to handle high-frequency time-series write volumes.
Trade-off Consideration: NoSQL sacrifices multi-document ACID transactions and complex relational joins in favor of write throughput and availability.

q-a3-3.examinerTip: Always balance an evaluation by discussing the trade-offs (e.g. eventual consistency vs strict relational constraints).

q-a4-1.prompt: Distinguish between supervised learning and unsupervised learning, providing one representative application for each.
q-a4-1.hint: Think about the presence or absence of labeled target output data.

markScheme.point: Supervised Learning: Trained on input-output pairs with known ground-truth labels (e.g. email spam classification, medical image diagnosis).
Unsupervised Learning: Discovers hidden patterns, clusters, or relationships in unlabeled data without explicit targets (e.g. customer market segmentation, anomaly detection).

q-a4-1.examinerTip: Clearly state the role of labeled training data.

q-a4-2.prompt: Explain the problem of overfitting in an artificial neural network and discuss two techniques used during training to mitigate it.
q-a4-2.hint: What happens when a model memorizes training noise instead of learning generalizable representations? Mention dropout, regularisation, or early stopping.

markScheme.point: Overfitting Explanation: The network fits the training dataset too closely, capturing random statistical noise and specific details, leading to poor generalization on unseen validation data.
Mitigation 1 (Dropout): Randomly deactivates a fraction of neurons during each forward-backward training pass, forcing the network to learn redundant, co-adapted representations.
Mitigation 2 (Early Stopping): Monitors performance against a separated validation set and halts training iterations once validation loss begins to diverge.
Alternative Mitigation (Data Augmentation / L2 Regularization): Penalisies large weight vectors or artificially expands sample diversity.

q-a4-2.examinerTip: Illustrate with the relationship between training error (continuously drops) and validation error (starts rising).

q-a4-3.prompt: Discuss two sources of algorithmic bias in an automated university admissions screening model, and state one measure to audit for fairness.
q-a4-3.hint: Consider historical human training bias and underrepresentation in the dataset.

markScheme.point: Historical Training Bias: Historical admissions data reflects past human prejudices and systemic inequities which the algorithm codifies and amplifies.
Sampling Underrepresentation: If minority demographics are sparsely represented in training cohorts, the model produces higher variance and erroneous rejections.
Fairness Audit: Perform demographic parity testing or counterfactual evaluation across protected characteristics to measure disparate impact.

q-a4-3.examinerTip: Ensure you address both the training data genesis and algorithmic mitigation.

q-cs-2027-1.prompt:
Visionary Studios is evaluating the computational requirements of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) for generating client advertising drafts.

(a) Outline the role of the Markov chain and Gaussian noise schedule during the forward diffusion process. [2 marks]

(b) Explain why the reverse denoising process creates a computational latency bottleneck when generating high-resolution images, and explain how a modern scheduler (e.g. DDIM) mitigates this latency. [2 marks]
q-cs-2027-1.hint: Consider the predetermined variance schedule beta_t in forward diffusion vs the sequential iterative evaluation of the U-Net in reverse sampling.

markScheme.point: (a) Forward Process: In forward diffusion, Gaussian noise is iteratively injected into an image over T discrete timesteps according to a predetermined noise schedule (beta_t). The Markov property ensures each noisy state x_t depends solely on the immediate previous state x_(t-1), asymptotically transforming the image into pure isotropic Gaussian noise.

(b) Reverse Bottleneck: The reverse denoising process cannot jump straight to the clean image; the neural network (U-Net) must be executed iteratively across all timesteps (e.g., T=1000) to estimate and subtract noise step-by-step, demanding significant GPU FLOPs and wall-clock latency per generation.

(b) Scheduler Mitigation: Non-Markovian deterministic schedulers (such as Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models - DDIM) skip intermediate steps during inference, enabling high-fidelity image synthesis in as few as 20 to 50 steps instead of 1000, slashing production latency for client drafts.

q-cs-2027-1.examinerTip: Distinguish clearly between the forward process (which has an analytical closed-form jump during training) and the reverse process (which is strictly sequential during inference).

q-cs-2027-3.unitName: 2027 Case Study: Generative AI for Image Creation
q-cs-2027-3.subtopicName: GAN Training Stability & Mode Collapse (HL Only)
q-cs-2027-3.prompt:
Visionary Studios machine learning team is experimenting with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate rapid photorealistic textures for concept art backgrounds.

(a) Describe the adversarial zero-sum dynamic between the Generator and the Discriminator during GAN training. [2 marks]

(b) Explain the phenomenon of mode collapse in GANs, citing how it would negatively impact Visionary Studios advertising campaigns. [2 marks]

(c) Outline two mathematical or architectural strategies used to stabilize GAN training and mitigate mode collapse. [2 marks]
q-cs-2027-3.hint: Focus on the minimax objective, latent-to-data mapping, diversity reduction, and Wasserstein loss with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP).

markScheme.point: (a) Adversarial Dynamic: The Generator maps a d-dimensional noise vector z to synthetic images G(z) aiming to minimize log(1 - D(G(z))) to deceive the Discriminator. Simultaneously, the Discriminator is trained to maximize log D(x) + log(1 - D(G(z))), classifying real images x as 1 and fake images G(z) as 0 in a two-player zero-sum minimax optimization.

(b) Mode Collapse: Mode collapse occurs when the Generator learns to output only a narrow subset of realistic images that consistently trick the Discriminator, rather than learning the full distribution. For Visionary Studios, this results in repetitive, non-diverse concept art (e.g. generating only one car model or one face type across all prompts), failing client creative briefs.

(c) Strategy 1 - Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP): Replaces standard Jensen-Shannon divergence with Earth Mover's Distance (Wasserstein metric) and enforces 1-Lipschitz continuity via gradient penalty, eliminating vanishing gradients and ensuring continuous informative gradient feedback.

(c) Strategy 2 - Minibatch Discrimination / Feature Matching: Equips the Discriminator with information across all samples in a batch to detect lack of diversity, penalizing the Generator if sample variance collapses.

q-cs-2027-3.examinerTip: Higher Level Section B questions require exact understanding of why the Discriminator overpowering the Generator causes vanishing gradients, and how Earth Mover's Distance solves it.

q-cs-2027-4.unitName: 2027 Case Study: Generative AI for Image Creation
q-cs-2027-4.subtopicName: Quantitative Model Evaluation: FID vs Inception Score (HL Only)
q-cs-2027-4.prompt:
Visionary Studios needs a quantitative methodology to benchmark the quality and diversity of images produced by candidate generative models before deploying them into client workflows.

(a) Contrast how the Inception Score (IS) and the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) evaluate synthetic images. [3 marks]

(b) Explain why Visionary Studios should prioritize FID over IS when benchmarking commercial advertising image generation models. [3 marks]
q-cs-2027-4.hint: Consider reference vs reference-free metrics, conditional entropy vs feature-space Gaussian statistics (mean and covariance), and sensitivity to mode collapse.

markScheme.point: (a) Inception Score (IS): Evaluates ONLY generated images using a pre-trained Inception-v3 classifier. It measures fidelity via low conditional entropy (sharp, recognizable objects) and diversity via high marginal entropy across classes. Crucially, IS never compares generated images against real training images.

(a) Fréchet Inception Distance (FID): Extracts deep feature representations from the penultimate layer of Inception-v3 for BOTH real and generated datasets, fitting multivariate Gaussian distributions (mean mu and covariance matrix Sigma) and computing the Wasserstein-2 / Fréchet distance between them. Lower FID indicates higher fidelity and distribution similarity.

(b) Reason 1 - Direct Reference Comparison: Unlike IS, FID explicitly checks whether the generated images mirror the statistical distribution of real commercial assets; if a model creates beautiful but unrepresentative images, FID penalizes it.

(b) Reason 2 - Mode Collapse Detection: If the model suffers from mode collapse and outputs only one category or style, IS can still report a falsely high score if outputs are sharp, whereas FID immediately detects the covariance collapse (Sigma_g mismatch) and produces a poor score.
(b) Reason 3 - Robustness to Artifacts: FID is much more sensitive to subtle perceptual artifacts, noise injection errors, and blur, mirroring human visual perception much better than IS.

q-cs-2027-4.examinerTip: State the scoring direction clearly: higher IS is better, but lower FID is better (0 indicates identical distributions).

q-cs-2027-5.unitName: 2027 Case Study: Generative AI for Image Creation
q-cs-2027-5.subtopicName: Hybrid Latent Diffusion vs Pixel-Space Evaluation (HL Only)
q-cs-2027-5.prompt:
Visionary Studios currently relies on pixel-space diffusion models to generate concept art and commercial advertising assets. While the visual fidelity is high, the generation latency (up to 45 seconds per 1024x1024 image) and massive GPU memory footprint on workstation graphics cards bottleneck creative velocity.

The studio's AI Director proposes adopting a Hybrid Latent Diffusion Model (combining a Variational Autoencoder [VAE] for spatial compression with a latent-space U-Net conditioned via CLIP cross-attention).

Evaluate this proposal for Visionary Studios. In your response, address:
- Architectural mechanisms (VAE perceptual compression, latent diffusion, and text-conditioning)
- Computational performance, hardware feasibility, and latency benefits
- Creative limitations, artifacts, and trade-offs
- A synthesized strategic recommendation for Visionary Studios' production pipeline. [12 marks]
q-cs-2027-5.hint: Structure your 12-mark answer across: (1) Architecture, (2) Computational advantages, (3) Limitations & failure modes, and (4) Contextualized studio recommendation with two-tiered pipeline.

markScheme.point: Architectural Mechanisms (3 marks): VAE Encoder compresses high-dimensional pixel space (H x W x 3) by a factor of 8 (e.g. 64x spatial area reduction) into a compact latent space representation (h x w x c), removing imperceptible high-frequency noise while retaining core semantics. Iterative forward/reverse diffusion is executed exclusively in this compressed latent space via a U-Net. A CLIP text encoder converts prompts into text embeddings, which are injected into the U-Net through cross-attention layers to steer generation. Finally, the VAE Decoder reconstructs the high-resolution pixel image from the denoised latent vector.

Computational & Hardware Feasibility (3 marks): Performing denoising in latent space reduces the tensor dimension processed by each attention and convolutional layer by roughly 64-fold, leading to dramatic reductions in floating-point operations (FLOPs) and VRAM usage. This slashes inference latency from ~45s down to 2-4s, enabling designers to execute iterative prompt prototyping locally on standard high-end studio workstations without constantly renting high-cost cloud clusters.

Limitations & Creative Trade-offs (3 marks): The VAE compression is lossy; high-frequency fine details (e.g. legible typography, micro-textures, intricate hands and eyes) can suffer from blur or latent reconstruction distortions. Cross-attention conditioning can suffer from prompt leakage (attribute binding errors where adjectives attach to the wrong nouns). Additionally, a multi-stage pipeline introduces compound failure points where a defect in the VAE decoder ruins an otherwise pristine latent generation.

Synthesized Strategic Recommendation (3 marks): Visionary Studios should adopt the Hybrid Latent Diffusion model as their primary tier for creative ideation, client concept boards, and rapid iterative exploration. To resolve the high-frequency detail limitations on final client deliverables, the studio should implement a two-tiered pipeline: fast latent diffusion for drafting, followed by a selective high-resolution upscaling pass (using pixel-space refinement or a GAN-based super-resolution perceptual enhancer) combined with mandatory C2PA content provenance watermarking.

q-cs-2027-5.examinerTip: In the Paper 1 Section B 12-mark evaluation question, high-scoring responses provide balanced criteria with specific operational solutions (e.g., two-tiered pipeline, C2PA watermarks, FLOPs/VRAM reduction) rather than vague opinions.

q-synoptic-a1-a2-1.prompt:
Trace the step-by-step sequence of operations that take place between a computer's hardware (CPU, RAM, System Bus) and the operating system network stack when an incoming packet arrives at the Network Interface Card (NIC) over a Local Area Network (LAN).

In your response, refer explicitly to:
- Direct Memory Access (DMA) and the packet buffer in RAM
- The Interrupt Request (IRQ) line
- The CPU's context save and Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
- The operating system protocol stack handling. [4 marks]
q-synoptic-a1-a2-1.hint: Trace the flow from physical packet arrival at the NIC, DMA transfer into primary RAM, raising an IRQ, CPU pausing its fetch-execute cycle to execute the ISR, and passing the packet up the OSI/TCP-IP stack.

markScheme.point: Packet Ingestion & DMA: The NIC receives frame bits from the physical medium, validates the checksum (CRC), and transfers the packet directly into an allocated kernel ring buffer in RAM via Direct Memory Access (DMA) without loading the CPU [1 mark].
Interrupt Signaling: The NIC triggers an Interrupt Request (IRQ) signal along the control bus to notify the CPU that packet data is available in primary memory [1 mark].

Context Save & ISR Dispatch: The CPU completes its current machine instruction, pushes register states (Program Counter, Accumulator, Status Register) onto the system stack, and vectors to the Network Driver Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) [1 mark].

Protocol Demultiplexing: The ISR clears the hardware interrupt and hands the packet off to the OS network stack, which strips Ethernet, IP, and TCP headers before queuing data for the target application socket [1 mark].

(b) Outline why the customer grouping cannot use supervised learning. [3]

(c) Outline why the van routing improves over time while the email classifier does not. [3]
q-a4-09.hint: Categorize unsupervised clustering, supervised classification, and reinforcement learning. Contrast static training boundaries with active environment feedback.

markScheme.point:
(a) Grouping customers: Unsupervised learning (clustering).
Predicting email category: Supervised learning (classification).
Improving van delivery routes: Reinforcement learning.

(b) Supervised learning requires pre-existing labeled output targets for each input instance; in customer segmentation, the retailer has no predefined ground-truth groups or explicit labels, meaning the algorithm must uncover latent clusters autonomously from purchasing attributes.

(c) Reinforcement learning continuously updates its policy in response to ongoing environmental trial-and-error rewards (traffic conditions, delivery delays), whereas a standard supervised email classifier operates on fixed weights frozen after training unless manually retrained on newly labeled datasets.

q-a4-09.examinerTip: For 9-mark multi-part questions, ensure each sub-part explicitly references the given scenario context (customers, emails, delivery vans).

q-a4-11.prompt:

Equity & Digital Oligopoly: The exorbitant financial capital required creates an extreme compute divide, monopolizing frontier AI development within a few multinational corporations and excluding academic institutions, non-profits, and the Global South from shaping foundational technologies.

q-a4-11.examinerTip: Do not treat this as purely an environmental question; address both the ecological footprint and the geopolitical/economic equity imbalance.

q-a4-12.prompt:
A recruitment company trains a model on ten years of its own hiring decisions. It removes gender and ethnicity from the data before training. Applications from certain groups are still rejected at a much higher rate.

(a) Explain why removing those fields did not prevent the disparity. [4]

(b) Outline why the disparity is harder to detect once the fields have been removed. [2]

(c) Outline what the company should do instead. [2]
q-a4-12.hint: Investigate proxy variables, blind auditing obstacles, and proactive debiasing techniques.

markScheme.point: (a) Proxy variables / Latent feature correlation: Other input features (such as school attended, postal code, sports, extracurriculars, or phrasing in resumes) strongly correlate with gender and ethnicity; the model learns to associate these proxies with historical hiring bias embedded in the ten-year training decisions.

(b) Without demographic attributes attached to validation predictions, the company cannot easily compute stratified performance metrics (e.g., disparate impact ratio or false rejection rates across sub-populations), masking institutional discrimination under a guise of 'blind' neutrality.

(c) Retain sensitive demographic labels exclusively for fairness auditing and algorithmic stress-testing; actively debias historical training labels, retrain on curated balanced datasets, and implement human-in-the-loop review.

q-a4-12.examinerTip: This is a classic algorithmic bias question. Define 'proxy variable' explicitly in part (a).

q-a4-13.prompt: (a) A government proposes using machine learning to identify benefit claims likely to be fraudulent. Discuss this proposal. [5]
q-a4-13.hint: Balance administrative efficiency and taxpayer savings against false accusation risks, systemic bias against vulnerable citizens, and due process/appeal guarantees.

markScheme.point: Benefits / Efficiency: Automated pattern recognition can rapidly analyze massive transaction volumes, flag suspicious inconsistencies, reduce bureaucratic processing costs, and safeguard public funds against organized fraud.

Risks / Harm: False positives unfairly cut off essential survival stipends for vulnerable families; historical audit data often over-samples marginalized communities, training algorithms that disproportionately suspect the disadvantaged.
Governance Conclusion: Automated flagging must require independent human caseworker investigation, robust explainability, and accessible legal appeal mechanisms before benefits are suspended.

q-a4-13.examinerTip: For 'Discuss' command terms, present a balanced appraisal with both benefits and severe ethical hazards before concluding.

q-a4-15.prompt: (a) A messaging platform ranks, filters and auto-replies to its users' messages. Identify two ethical issues raised by the use of machine learning in online communication. [2]

q-a4-16.prompt:
Current systems protect data in transit using encryption methods that rely on certain calculations being computationally infeasible.

(a) Outline one security threat that quantum computing poses to systems designed in this way. [2]
q-a4-16.hint: Consider Shor's algorithm breaking asymmetric cryptography like RSA or ECC by solving prime factorization in polynomial time.

markScheme.point: Quantum computers utilizing Shor's algorithm can solve discrete logarithm and prime factorization problems in polynomial time.

This renders ubiquitous asymmetric public-key cryptography (such as RSA and Diffie-Hellman/ECC) obsolete, enabling adversaries to decrypt captured encrypted communications (harvest now, decrypt later).

q-a4-16.examinerTip: Mention the theoretical basis (prime factorization / discrete logarithms) and the practical consequence (public key encryption failure).

q-a4-17.prompt:

q-a4-17.hint: Analyze economic productivity and consumer prices vs worker redundancy, regional unemployment, retraining programs, and safety.

q-a4-21.prompt:
A smart agriculture system uses machine learning to predict crop yields, detect plant diseases, and optimize irrigation schedules based on sensor data and weather patterns.

markScheme.point: (a) Edge devices process telemetry locally on-site without relying on continuous internet connectivity, overcoming the unreliable cellular/satellite bandwidth common in remote agricultural fields while eliminating cloud transmission latency.

q-a4-22.prompt:
A school district uses a supervised learning algorithm to predict which students are at risk of failing their final examinations. Teachers are encouraged to focus extra support on students flagged by the system.

(a) Identify two ethical concerns that might arise from using this supervised learning algorithm in education. [2]

(b) Explain two measures the school district could take to reduce the risk of harm from labelling while still using the predictions to support students. [4]

(a) Perpetuation of socioeconomic bias: Historical grading data may reflect institutional inequalities, causing minority or lower-income students to be flagged at disproportionate rates.

(b) Confidentiality and Positive Framing: Keep model risk scores private from students and peers, framing support interventions around constructive skill clinics rather than remedial or punitive tracking.

(b) Holistic Human Oversight: Require teachers and counselors to review qualitative student progress and personal circumstances before applying interventions, ensuring algorithms never trigger automated academic tracking.

q-a4-23.hint: Differentiate physical proximity to data generation, compute power, and network dependence.

markScheme.point: Edge Device: Low-power embedded hardware located directly at the site of data collection (e.g., in the vineyard fields) performing localized, real-time inference with minimal latency and without requiring constant network connectivity.

Cloud Platform: Scalable remote server clusters with high compute/storage capacity suitable for heavy model training and centralized multi-source analytics, accessible over high-bandwidth internet connections.

q-a4-23.examinerTip: Contrast physical location (on-site vs remote datacenters) and compute scale (constrained inference vs massive elastic training capacity).

q-a4-24.prompt:

(b) Strict Data Retention and Immediate Purging: Automatically delete biometric scans of individuals who do not match the target criminal database immediately upon capture, preventing mass surveillance databases.

(b) Mandatory Human Verification & Independent Audits: Require certified human biometric examiners to verify any algorithmic alert before law enforcement intervention, backed by recurring third-party fairness audits.

q-a4-25.prompt:

q-a4-26.prompt:
A bank replaces its loan officers with a model that approves or refuses applications automatically. An applicant refused a loan asks why.

(a) State the ethical principle the applicant is appealing to. [1]

(b) Outline why the bank may be unable to answer. [3]

markScheme.point: (a) The right to explanation / algorithmic transparency.

q-a4-27.prompt: (a) A fraud model rejects a transaction and no one can determine which factors caused it. Outline why a model that cannot explain its decisions is described as a security as well as an ethical concern. [3]

Auditability & Maintenance: Prevents cybersecurity auditors from debugging model failures, testing edge cases, or validating that security compliance standards are met.

q-a4-30.prompt:
A supermarket chain wants to improve operations using machine learning (ML). It plans two features:
- grouping customers based on purchase behaviour to design targeted promotions
- using an in-store camera system to detect when shelves are running low (near real-time)

(a) Outline one key characteristic of each of the following approaches:
- supervised learning
- unsupervised learning
- reinforcement learning [3]

(b) Describe how unsupervised learning could be used to group customers based on their shopping behaviour. [4]

(c) Explain two differences in hardware requirements between deploying the shelf-monitoring model on an edge device in the store and deploying it on a cloud-based platform. [4]
q-a4-30.hint: Outline the three core paradigms, detail clustering algorithms (k-means/hierarchical) with transaction vectors, and contrast local edge GPU/accelerator power and bandwidth with centralized cloud instances.

markScheme.point:
(a) Supervised Learning: Trained using paired input data and explicit ground-truth labels to minimize prediction loss.
Unsupervised Learning: Analyzes unlabeled data to detect latent patterns, distributions, or groupings without predefined target outputs.
Reinforcement Learning: An agent iteratively learns an optimal policy through exploratory actions, receiving feedback via scalar rewards and penalties from an environment.

(b) Feature extraction: Customer transactions are transformed into numerical vectors (e.g., spend amount, visit frequency, categories purchased).
Clustering: An algorithm (e.g., k-means) computes geometric distances between customer data points in multi-dimensional feature space, grouping customers with similar buying patterns together so customized marketing incentives can be directed to each cluster.

(c) Edge Deployment: Requires dedicated on-premise hardware accelerators (e.g., low-power tensor processing chips, local GPUs) installed in-store to handle real-time multi-camera video frame inferencing locally without saturating external network bandwidth.
Cloud Deployment: The store requires high-bandwidth upload network hardware and switches to continuously stream multi-camera video feeds, while the computation runs on elastic, high-memory virtualized cloud server clusters with centralized maintenance.

q-a4-30.examinerTip: In part (b), mention feature vectors and geometric distance/clustering in multi-dimensional space to secure top-band marks.
